newsitem.title: USA: FCC denies Perot request for more TV prime time.
newsitem.headline: FCC denies Perot request for more TV prime time.

text.p: In another setback for Ross Perot, regulators said on Friday they rejected a request by the Texas billionaire to force big television networks to sell him more prime time for his struggling presidential campaign.

The Federal Communications Commission, in a 4 to 0 vote on a complaint filed last week by Perot, said the networks acted legally by refusing to sell the Reform Party candidate extra prime time slots for his half-hour campaign infomercials.
Separately, a federal appeals court could rule as soon as Friday on Perot's request to block the upcoming presidential debates unless he participates. A U.S. judge denied the request Tuesday.
Perot and running mate Pat Choate are stuck at around five percent in the polls.

In his FCC complaint, Perot charged that ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox refused to sell him "reasonable" air time. He alleged that the networks broke a federal law ensuring that candidates have equal opportunity to appear on TV when their opponents appear, and that candidates get "reasonable access" to the airwaves.

He cited, among other elements, the coverage President Clinton and Republican Bob Dole received at their parties' nominating conventions in August, plus the air time both will get in the debates, which begin on Sunday in Hartford, Conn.
But the FCC said the networks were exempt from the equal opportunities provision of the law because the Clinton and Dole appearances were "bona fide" news programming.

The agency also said the networks had "properly balanced" Perot's request with their concerns about major programme disruptions. It added that the amount of time the networks offered "satisfied their 'reasonable access' obligations."
A Perot spokesman was not immediately available for comment.
Perot asked to buy eight half-hour prime time slots from each network -- beginning on Sept. 8 and continuing through the week of Oct. 27 -- plus time on the eve of the election.
Each network offered Perot a package of time, including a half hour of prime time in the month before the election.
Perot had urged the FCC to require the networks to sell him a "reasonable number" of prime time at the cheapest possible rate in the final weeks of the campaign.
The Perot camp noted in its complaint that in 1992 ABC, CBS and NBC sold Perot "significant amounts" of prime time as part of a campaign that cost him at least $60 million.
